problem: Existing zero-shot VLN methods in continuous environments couple high-level directional reasoning with low-level local grounding in a single waypoint/action decision, often rely on extra waypoint predictors, and use repeatedly summarized memory that loses detail.
motivation: Humans first look around to pick a direction and then look down to choose where to step. Coupled decisions make it hard to isolate and correct errors from direction ambiguity versus local target inaccuracy, which hurts in cluttered continuous environments.
key_idea: Decompose zero-shot VLN into panoramic direction selection followed by pixel-level target grounding on a downward-tilted view, with sliding-window dialogue memory and a reflective abort-and-reselect loop, all through prompting a Qwen3-VL model.
insight: Each component adds gains in the ablation: the P2D visual design lifts SR 26.0->29.0, SDM to 42.0, and RRM to 50.0 (100-episode subset). A history window of 1 works best (0 degrades, 2/4 give no gain), so a small amount of recent visual context suffices. RRM fires on only 4.7% of steps yet recovers 98.0% (49/50) of failure-prone decisions, cutting stuck decisions 113->51 and bad selections 60->13. Small models (2B) fail, so grounding capability matters.
method: P2D stage 1 (panoramic direction selection): six 60° RGB views are stitched into a panorama with view-index labels; the VLM outputs STOP or MOVE_TO_VIEW(k) given instruction and memory.

P2D stage 2 (downview local grounding): the direction-aligned RGB view tilted 15° downward is given to the VLM, which predicts a pixel target; it is projected to world coordinates with depth and executed by a low-level controller.

SDM (Sliding-Window Dialogue Memory): the episode is a multi-turn system/user/assistant dialogue; only the most recent W=1 steps keep images, older turns keep text decisions only, bounding visual context (peak CUDA memory increment 9.8 GB -> 2.1 GB).

RRM (Reflective Reorientation Mechanism): stage 2 can output abort(reason) when the downview lacks reliable evidence; the rejected direction and reason are written to memory (text only) and stage 1 re-selects excluding rejected directions, with a budget equal to the number of views.
Implementation: training-free prompting of Qwen3-VL (32B default; 2B/4B/8B evaluated), 224x224 inputs, Habitat, single A800 GPU.

setting.backbone: Qwen3-VL-32B (frozen, zero-shot prompting); 2B/4B/8B variants also tested
setting.observation: egocentric RGB (six 60° views stitched into a panorama, plus a 15° downward-tilted RGB view) with depth for pixel projection
setting.action_space: predicted pixel target projected to a world-coordinate waypoint, executed by a low-level controller in continuous space

numbers_note: Design-analysis results (panorama views, downview angle, window size) are given only in figures. The paper does not specify which 100 episodes were used.
results: On full R2R-CE val-unseen, P2DNav (32B) gets 40.2 SR / 62.7 OSR / 6.51 NE, beating CA-Nav (25.3 SR, waypoint-free) and NavGPT-CE (16.3 SR, waypoint-based), i.e. +58.9% and +146.6% relative. On the 100-episode subset it reaches 50.0 SR / 30.6 SPL versus SmartWay 29.0 / 22.5 and Open-Nav-Llama3.1 16.0 / 12.9. It still trails supervised models such as CLASH (65.0 SR) and ETPNav.
limitations: Still well below supervised methods (e.g. CLASH 65.0 SR, ETPNav 57.0 SR); on the full split SPL is only 24.1.
Failure modes are wrong panoramic direction selection and imprecise local targets near turns and intersections; small models (2B) perform poorly, and the approach depends on a large VLM.
Comparisons partly use a 100-episode subset, and only R2R-CE is evaluated.
